draft.title: Factorising non-monic quadratics
card: A non-monic quadratic has an \(x^{2}\) term with a coefficient other than 1, such as \(2x^{2} + 7x + 3\). Always take out any common factor first.
For \(ax^{2} + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to \(a \times c\) and add to \(b\). For \(2x^{2} + 7x + 3\), \(a \times c = 6\) and \(b = 7\), so the numbers are 1 and 6.
Split the middle term: \(2x^{2} + x + 6x + 3\). Factorise the first pair and the last pair: \(x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1)\).
Take out the common bracket: \((2x + 1)(x + 3)\). Check by expanding: \(2x^{2} + 6x + x + 3 = 2x^{2} + 7x + 3\).
draft.remember: Find two numbers that multiply to \(a \times c\) and add to \(b\), split the middle term, then take out the common bracket.

a.q: Which pair of numbers is used to split the middle term of \(3x^{2} + 10x + 8\)?
a.why: Here \(a \times c = 3 \times 8 = 24\) and \(b = 10\). The numbers 4 and 6 multiply to 24 and add to 10. The pair 1 and 8 multiplies to 8, which is just \(c\), but \(a\) must be included.
a.clue: Multiply the \(x^{2}\) coefficient by the constant first.

b.q: Which is the correct factorisation of \(6x^{2} + 13x + 5\)?
b.why: \(a \times c = 30\), and 3 and 10 multiply to 30 and add to 13. So \(6x^{2} + 3x + 10x + 5 = 3x(2x + 1) + 5(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)(3x + 5)\). The option \((2x + 5)(3x + 1)\) has the right terms in the wrong places: it expands to \(6x^{2} + 17x + 5\).
b.clue: Expand each option and compare the middle term with \(13x\).

check.summary: No problems found. Both questions have exactly one correct option, and the card, the explanations and all the expansions check out.
